context: Subgroup H of an ambient group G with operation restricted to H / group-substructure-inherited-operation
editorial_note: ProofWiki defines (H,∘) as a subgroup of an algebraic structure (G,∘) when H⊆G and (H,∘) is a group, explicitly allowing ambient non-group algebraic structures. This independent mathematical meaning deliberately specializes to an ambient GROUP G, the precise context needed by the earlier separately screened normal-subgroup and coset definitions. The same group operation must be inherited, not a new unrelated operation on H. Independently consulted ProofWiki One-Step Subgroup Test and Two-Step Subgroup Test, which show equivalent operational criteria when G is a group; these are THEOREMS supporting this specialization, not additional unread variant source assertions. In particular nonemptiness is essential in the subgroup tests, and the empty subset is not a subgroup of a group. Inverse and identity of the subgroup agree with ambient inverses and identity. A proper subgroup would require H≠G, not demanded here. ProofWiki notes a separate informal statistical sense of subgroup; deliberately not conflated. Source sections: Definition group-on-subset using same operation, Linked one- and two-step subgroup tests checked separately as theorems, Statistics sense explicitly rejected
text: Let (G,*) be a group and let H⊆G. The subset H is a subgroup of G if H equipped with the restriction of * to H×H is itself a group; the same binary operation is used.

context: Left coset of H in group G by g / left-multiply-subgroup
editorial_note: ProofWiki directly gives left coset as x∘H={x∘h:h∈H} and right coset as H∘x={h∘x:h∈H}, under a common operation. The page permits a more general ambient algebraic structure, but these independently reviewed versions RESTRICT to an ambient GROUP G and subgroup H≤G. In a nonabelian group with H not normal, gH and Hg can differ. Thus left and right cosets are distinct contexts under the same term group, not automatically equivalent formulations, though they coincide for every g if and only if H is normal. Cosets are SUBSETS of G; gH depends on a representative but multiple representatives may specify the same set. The set of all cosets is a coset SPACE, not itself one coset. Group quotient multiplication defined by (aH)(bH)=(ab)H is not generally well defined unless H is normal, a separate hypothesis retained in the earlier quotient-group definition. Source also notes rare notation reversal by author; mathematical operand direction controls these forms. Source sections: Left Coset, Right Coset, Source generality allows ambient non-group structure but current forms restrict to group
text: For a group G, subgroup H≤G and g∈G, the left coset of H represented by g is gH={gh:h∈H}, a subset of G.

context: Finite-limit convergence of real-valued series by partial sums / partial-sums-converge-to-real-limit
editorial_note: ProofWiki explicitly defines convergence of a series by convergence of its sequence of partial sums; its standard-number-field section covers Q, R and C, and the current meaning restricts to REAL terms and FINITE REAL sum. The index begins at n=0 here, differing harmlessly from the source's n=1 by relabeling; the substance is finite partial sums converging to an element of R. This does NOT mean absolute convergence: series can converge conditionally. A diverging-to-+infinity partial sum sequence is not convergent as a series in R. Convergence depends on the ORDER of terms and is not an unordered set sum. The general topological semigroup and normed-vector-space presentations in the source would need separately scoped meanings if admitted later; they are not equivalent to the current real-valued meaning across all structures. The source's partial-sum sequence and finite-limit criterion are independently supported by the explicitly cited real number topology, not a formal algebraic power-series coefficient object. Source sections: Convergent Series in a Number Field, General Definition by partial-sum convergence, Divergent Series
text: For a real sequence (a_n)_{n≥0}, the series ∑_{n=0}^∞a_n converges if there exists s∈ℝ such that the finite partial sums s_N=∑_{n=0}^N a_n tend to s as N→∞; then its sum equals s.

context: Real power series in variable x around specified real center ξ / centered-real-coefficient-power-series
editorial_note: ProofWiki defines a real power series centered at ξ∈R by ∑_{n≥0}a_n(x−ξ)^n with REAL coefficients and real variable, without stipulating convergence for every x. Its displayed center-zero form ∑a_nx^n is a SPECIAL CASE of the center-parameterized definition rather than a purported equivalent expression to any given nonzero-center series. We therefore admit the general-center definition once, and record the special-case formula only in the source review. The notation 'formal series expression' here describes the unevaluated summation syntax, NOT a claim that the object is necessarily an element of a separately-defined algebra R[[x]], since the page is about analytic power series and their convergence. The series always converges at its center ξ by convention for exponent n=0 and finite coefficient a0, while the convergence set can be smaller than all real numbers. The distinct previous generating-function meaning is an actual real-valued function on its convergence domain; do not collapse the series expression with its evaluated generating function. Source sections: General centered real power series, Also defined as center zero specialization
text: Given a real center ξ∈ℝ and coefficients (a_n)_{n≥0}⊆ℝ, the real power series centered at ξ is the formal series expression ∑_{n=0}^∞a_n(x−ξ)^n in the real variable x; convergence at x is not assumed.
